items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Thursday.
items.description:
Finally! They left the lights on

at night, and I could see what's in there.

And it's just what you would expect. An office. That's all. Someplace interchangeable with numberless other locales.

So that was exciting! Made my night last night, it did. That, and cleaning some North Dakota syrup off a wire-mesh expandable shelf, and deciding that a lot of the items in that particular cupboard can be put away for The Last House. Amusing, that, since I had originally intended to use them here. Three little glass pots of bespoke English jam I bought last December, thinking "I will go to the Hip New Place and I will have a croissant and this spread, and I will be having a civilized and well-composed existence." But I couldn't bring myself to use them. They look too nice sitting  on the shelf. So I'll move them to the next home and, I have no doubt whatsoever, not use them there, either.

I think Wednesday was the least productive day I've had in some time. I am not sure I'm bothered by that. I posted last night's work on the Substack, did ten motel postcards fro 2027 and six matchbooks, hit the gym, visited the Giant Swede, then decided I would have a Moscow Mule in the evening. I went to Lundsnbyerlys for Ginger Beer, which the app said they had. They did not.

SIGH

I'm beginning to rethink my decision not to get a Patriot-adjacent pizza.

Sorry, that's a crossover ep reference to Monday's Substack. The free one.

Anything else I can use to fill up the space before we get to the Prompt, which was occasioned by last Monday's Mummy rewatch? Well, I've had some colorized Architectural Record pictures hanging around, and this seems like a good time as any.

The Michigan Square Building, 1930. The original shot:

Colorized:

Seems about right.

We can't know what this hallway was like without actual color pictures.

Could be this.

I run it again and again and it comes up with different color schemes and hallucinates stores. Best to stick with something simple:

If everything had been in color since, oh, 1900, we'd see the past in a different way. To state the obvious.

This next one seemed to wonderful to be true, but again, it's possible.

It had to look like something more; why not this?

The building's gone, and if there are records, they're locked away, or lost.

ACH I forgot to tell you the connection between that NFL ad and the picture of Patrick Stewart. I'm sure someone got it in the comments, and bravo, or brava, if you did. The answer: the music under the ad . . .

. . . was the NFL Films number

The Equalizer

.

Patrick Stewart was shown as he appeared in the movie

Lifeforce.

I mean,

c'mon.

I was looking for reviews of The Mummy, and found this breezy entry. I liked the guy's style.

What caught my eye, of course, was the end.

E. de S. M.

That suggests he was so well known he could just use his initials. Or, there wasn't room for his full name. Or, he had always gone by his initials, as a trademark, a conceit.

It didn't take long to find out who he was: Edward deSelding Melcher.

Google's AI summary is helpful.

Born into a socially prominent New York family, Melcher was the son of Dr. and Mrs. John S. Melcher. He attended Harvard University as a member of the Class of 1928. During his time at Harvard, he was a highly active member of the famous Hasty Pudding Club, notably performing as a female impersonator in the club's theatrical productions, such as Not NowâLater.

Melcher built a reputation in journalism during the early 1930s as aÂ dramatic and motion picture criticÂ forÂ

The Washington Star

. In November 1936, he left the newspaper to pursue a career in Hollywood, where he worked as a scriptwriter forÂ RKO Pictures.

None of the AI bios note something I found in a 1936 paper:

Before we go to the movie, note that line at the end: "There is a little color cartoon about spring." Indeed there was, and is, and it's the first directorial effort by a fellow named William . . .

Hanna

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Wednesday.
items.description:
Sometimes the sky

looks like an armada, massed for great battle.

Sail t'wards the Hotel Kronos, lads, then starboard unto the Spanish Main

or something like that. This was the balcony view a few days ago. Today, bright skies and heat: 82 for the high. Ahhh, to wear a short-sleeved shirt in October.

Another view from the balcony: I'm not sure how this is going to work.

I could hang that in a museum, couldn't I? I suppose standards are debased enough. At least it's real! Although I could make a lot of money like the YouTube guys, who are really good at discovering unexplored subject matter. This guy found a niche:

This channel has AI animations set to AI music. Easy-listening stuff.

The same AI music channel has many videos devoted to retrofuture visions of a nuclear-powered 50s:

It's instantly convincing and instantly

off.

Most of it really doesn't make sense.

They're hoovering up the leaves with a machine that spits them back out:

What music fits this scene?

I wouldn't say "mellow trombone easy-listening 'jazz'" but that's what it is, and it's unlistenable. I tried. I tried a lot. The relationship between music and your brain ought to be like the two parts of Velcro, but in this case, one side is silk. Nothing catches.

I understand the appeal. I too wish it all had happened like that - except it wouldn't have lasted. The next generation would've rejected it all in favor of something

natural

and

organic

- and then

their

children would have embraced the chrome-and-turquoise robot aesthetic, and picked up old busted inert robots in thrift stores and estate sales, and sold them on eBay, with sad badly-lit pictures of the home-bots propped up against a basement wall like hostages.

Saw this the other day, a comment about an AI 70s mall-music compilation:

The Love Boat

was not wonderfully innocent.

Also: "We all shared such wonderful innocence," says

Bobbuttface108

, a name that presumes the existence of 107 other Bobbuttfaces.

Anyway. If you wish:

There's a lot of this stuff. I'm sure some hate it because it's AI, and a sliver of the population hates it on contact, because the ethos and settings aren't just dog whistles but absolute tornado sirens. In an actual

Clockwork Orange

society they'd use the Ludovico technique to make Alex physically ill at the sight of these things, he said, exaggerating. Somewhat.

One of the biggest problems with this imagined world, of course, is its suburban setting, and it's reliance on two great American sins: the straight line, and the curve.

As we will soon see.

Thereâs a certain âNew Yorker Toneâ that gripes my gums, as they used to say. Itâs smart and smug and full of assumptions about what good smart people think. There was a piece that reviewed books on zoning and urban design, and the author seemed to think that arranging things by straight lines was amusing in that empty naive optimistic American way, and then arranging things with curved streets was amusing, in that empty naive optimistic American way. Both were attempts by white people to bring order to the land they had stolen. The review ended thus:

Specht calls for a truce between city and suburb. The government once dedicated itself energetically to distributing homesteads or homes.

He seems to conflate 19th century homestead acts with post-war policies that favored the burbs, which is different. VA loans were not

energetically distributing homes.

If such energy could go toward building up higher-density neighborhoods in lower-cost areas, a hitherto elusive âshared civic lifeâ might be obtained, Specht suggests.

High-density in lower-cost neighborhoods - what an idea. Totally bizarre that no oneâs tried it before.

"Shared civic life" does not come from density, but the culture of the people who inhabit the tall thick towers.

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Tuesday.
items.description:
Birch had another one. Itâs hard for me to discern the severity, since I donât know if I woke up in the middle, or the end. It was 2:45. Afterwards he was less disoriented than he used to be. I have a plan to get him focused: a Frosty Paws ice cream treat calms him down and puts him back in a familiar state of mind, it seems. He barked a bit but calmed down soon. We fell back asleep.

Woke to a gray day and a weary sad sense of inevitability, again. This is two in one month. One âbreakthroughâ per month is supposed to be okay. I thought,

well, itâs the end of the month,  maybe we can count this as the October Seizure.

I did the laundry to clean the dog bed and the towels. We took a long walk in the morning and I let him roam all over the field to find

le spot juste

. My shoes were soaked when we got back and the day laid ahead like a cold dead thing.

It got better. But. But. As with the last time, my mind goes ahead to next month, the one after that - I see him here, still okay, and then I consider the possibility that he will not be here. IF IT IS A BRAIN TUMOR. They said it wasnât epilepsy. Okay. Unlikely. But itâs been almost eleven months. Mind races around that one, discarding evidence and denying probabilities and all that. Heâs not fine but he is. Every day, heâs my Birch, with all his moods and habits and pleasures. Every morning heâs happy to go out, tail up, his ears bouncing up and down as we trot down the hallway. Lifeâs good!

You have to remember that heâs a dog, and hence is taking things as they come. He looks forward to things, of course. He anticipates them. When we went to the Edina Spine he walked to the place where he likes to drink, only to find it drained. There was a little deflation you can see in his ears:

He went to all the spots, and they were all dry.

We walked on until we got to the lake, and there he had a sip.  Back to the car, off on some errands. Back to the Fred, happy walk to the elevators, down the hall: it was that time of day when I had a few pieces of salami as a snack, and he would wait for a slice. Everything was good. After the nap it was warm enough to sit on the balcony with a cup of coffee, and of course he had to come out, nails clattering on the metal floor. After dinner we took our walk, and ran into the wild turkeys. They hadn't left, not yet.  He enjoyed his usual sniffing spots and found some new fascinating thread that dragged him into the great field. Then we went to the Yard, which is the space - literally, a yard, 3' X 3' - where he keeps his sticks,  and I finished my cigar and he toyed with a wet ripe log.

Horrid start and a perfect day.

It made me angry again, though. I do not like to be angry again. But it reminds me how I had told ETBF that he deserved to pass in his own backyard, his own home. (For that matter, so did I.) I suppose heâs lost the memory of that place. It plays no role in his life anymore. But it was his realm, his great big yard where he chased things and ran for sticks, and laid in the sun in the grass. Goddammit.

That's not the reason I don't want to have conversations with her, but it's one of them. Every subject has something burning in its core.

If he goes here, at the Fred, it will be horrible afterwards, empty and vacant. A lot of the brio I feel here will be gone. The

two-of-us-against-the-world

mood whenever we head out, and he looks up at me to make sure everythingâs jake, the little rituals of the day, the one-sided conversations - itâs miserable to imagine the loss.

It would be easier at The Last Place, the house I might buy, IF? I donât know. I love the view from Fred Base One, a lot; I like the conversations in the elevator, the liveliness of the place, the park right outside the door, the way the place is appointed. Maybe Iâll just stay. And then I think: that means

Here, and no further.

That just seems like THE END, with nothing of consequence to follow.

No, no, go get a house, and then . . . miss all the human society at the Fred.

Itâs been a long day. Iâm not tired. But Iâm tired.

LATER

That was last week. He's been fine since.

We also went to Centennial Lakes to our spot, which wasn't occupied today. Last time we visited, a couple was taking some engagement-announcement pictures. This did not dissuade him at all, because he was thirsty, and he crashed the scene to slake his thirst. I apologized, but they didn't care.

Sweet dog!

Everyone loves Birch.

More leftovers.

This

manhole enthusiast site says . . .

Apparently this is a coalhole.

Coal holes: These are covers from the period when the houses were heated with coal, into which the coal bags were poured, so that the coals did not have to enter the houses.Â

These lids were used in the 19th and early 20th centuries.

It always pays to look down as well as up when you're in a different city.

I am not yet weary in the slightest of the old

Outer Limits

, but I understand not everyone is fascinated with screengrabs of a 1963 show that lacks the quirks and twists of The Twilight Zone.  Therefore, as a reward for you,  we'll have a challenge after this installment, the subject of which will be familiar to keen students of Bleat obsessions.

Old anthology shows

are great places to find actors at the start of their careers, as well as explore how classic TV did more with less.

This grabs your attention right away:

And here you're wondering where we are, and why. Well, obviously on a sound stage on a episode with a limited budget. But what's the story?

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Monday.
items.description:
My only regret

about the three weeks of interruption of our Regularly Scheduled Programming is the missed opportunity to give you a look at how Fall has touched Sunderwood Park.

The feral plants were hit hard, and went stark brown quite quickly. A few trees followed the change in fashion:

Everything else was still mostly green. <newt_inflection> Mostly. </newt_inflection> The sun slams down hard, though, and our post-supper walks are either concluded in the dark or begun earlier, which means an earlier supper. The wild turkeys just . . . disappeared. All summer they numbered eight or nine, wandering around like idiots in the Pentagon parking lot. Theyâre just gone. I donât think they walked south. Itâs a mystery.

The week after I got back was happy. It was good to return to The Fred, and Birch was ecstatic that I had not vanished for good. As is usual, I woke early due to reverse jet lag, and would be pleased to find myself good to go  I like this! Itâs productive! And every day I slipped closer to my usual time. It reminded me of coming back after the October Trip, post-letter, when I rose at dawn and took Birch for a walk in the woods and felt preternaturally connected with everything I was going to lose, eventually. Ugh.

Little did I know it would end up in a year with some amount of satisfaction because the blood-red trivets had arrived.

When I started planning for the Hip New Place, I bought three yellow trivets, the idea being that the Fred would be monochrome with splashes of color. Mostly yellow for the main living space. But now that autumn is here, the bright sunny hues are out of place, so I bought the trivets again in an appropriate hue. They arrived today, according to the alert I got from the Amazon app, so letâs check the mailroom after the evening walk and get them. Can't find them. Ah: the app has a picture of where the guy left the box.

This isnât really as much help as you might think

But I found them. Also, matching coasters. Theyâll work through Christmas. After that?

After that?

Will I be starting to pull away from here, looking for the Last House?

Iâve been looking at the real estate sites again, and despairing. I donât want any of these places. Thereâs something drastically wrong with all of them. Youâre dealing with mid-century rambler Window Issues, wherein the main room has a huge window youâll have to keep closed - donât want to be on display - and the room Iâd use for an office has an odd tiny corner window. Iâm not saying I love my office now - I do not, itâs the main failing of Fred Base One aside from the closets - but smaller rooms with limited windows donât feel right.

It used to feel right. I used to have an office I loved. With unique windows.  I used to have a proper house. FARG YOU, FORMER.

As I write this itâs 12:37 AM and the silly fillies above have been thumping for almost an hour now. I do not know what they are doing. Some sort of dance party, perhaps. Back and forth, thump thump thump, as though itâs 1957 and theyâre secretaries being chased around the desk by a leering boss. On the other hand, I love my view, the light, the mornings and sunsets, the access to Sunderwood Park, the solidity and conviviality of this place. BUT to stay is to rot, in a way. To give up. Last stop before the boneyard.

Then I go over to the Giant Swedeâs and see all the things he has to do to keep the place intact, and think âwhy would I take on all these responsibilitiesâ and worry about peeling paint on a corner of an eave, but then I think n

o, I would like to mow a lawn agai

n. I really would. It was a great task at Jasperwood, and I got in trouble if I expressed exhaustion at any point, since this was seen as a sign of SOMETHING BAD that went to the HEART OF MY CHARACTER. It would be nice just to mow the lawn and say âwhewâ at the end of it and have a Saturday beer and not get excoriated because my âwhewâ indicated I felt put upon and resentful that I had to do something.

Maybe I'll have a Guinness after I do the lawn. I felt a deep need for a Guinness after I got back, and as you might expect I had none on hand. This meant I should buy some. Iâd been drinking stout at the Anchor all week, an Adnams stout, and I liked it a lot. Off to Infinite Spirits - where we will spend every single sent of our class-action lawsuit settlement!

All thirty-three dollars!

From Apple, of all places. They had announced their AI capabilities then delivered a device that didnât meet what theyâd promised, and hence the class-action suit. Apple paid off some go-away money and I was sent a check for $33. I traded it for Guinness and a bottle of Lismore at Traders Joe. It is a delicious Speyside, ridiculous price for the quality, and I learned itâs owned by Grantâs. As long as youâre up, get me a Lismore!

Anyway. Houses. Do I want to dine in this room?

I do not want to dine in this room, unless I am Up North and this is my cabin.

Does it have the hated stove?

It has the hated stove.

Do I want to buy something whose upper story has a room where you suddenly find yourself in a happier version of the Twin Peaks Black Lodge, and have to sit down and await your fate in a realm where time does not seem to move at all?

I do not. Do I want a basement thatâs a cheerful version of the Backrooms? No I do not want a basement thatâs a cheerful version of the Backrooms

I don't have to make a decision at the moment. For a while. Be patient.

By the way, I'm having a Guiness right now. It's delicious. Talked to daughter for two hours tonight, a perfect end to a quiet weekend. Now to the workweek! With this entry, it's one piece down, eleven to go. I love retirement. Really! I do!

A few leftovers. Why not.

I remember where I took this one, so it was easy to find on the map. It's the side of the Netherlands Embassy.

Look at this magnificent pile:

The Victoria & Albert Museum. Civilizations don't

have

to build these things, you know. It's laudable when they do, and it means even more when they're meant for the citizens. For edification and ennoblement.

In keeping with our Monday tradition, which became a "tradition" for reasons I can't recall and probably don't matter, we continue with our Monday trademark. For this year we'll do 1936.

Rox, as in mountains, I guess.

If anything sums up the early 20th century the immigrant experience, it's this: "Seplowitz Bros., doing business as Britton Company of America."

You know you're in for a good classic monster movie when you hear the plane.

I've done these before, but not like this. We're going to do

ancillary media impact,

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Tuesday.
items.description:
TODAY IS SPICED AMBER DAY

On the train, post Ipswich switch. The return trip isnât as fraught, since you arrive at Platform One and leave on Two, which is on the same side of the station. No schlepping. The problem I always encounter, but will never encounter again,  is that the down train for Stratford leaves on platform 2, and there doesnât seem to be a platform 2. Thereâs 2A, 2B, 2C, but nothing thatâs just two. Thatâs because this train is long enough to encompass the entirety of 2. It contains multitudes. It gathers up A B and C into its arms and unifies the entire platform with a single purpose. Really, we could learn a lot from it.

Now we are between Colchester and the final destination, London Liverpool, but Iâm getting off at Stratford to snag the Lizzwhiz to the bowels of Heathrow. Beautiful day to travel. Blue skies and the sort of warmth-undercut-by-fleeting-cold you get in the early fall.

Itâs a lot of training today. East Anglia to the London area, tube to Heathrow, check in at hotel, back to London for early supper, back to hotel. Worth it if the payoutâs Dishoom.

Back later with more exciting rail-related updates.

LATER

To relief of all, I have no updates. But I have a 20 second recap.

After I checked in I went back through the walkway, which I have now dubbed Dalmatian Alley, due to its poor paint condition.

Really, Heathrow. Letting the side down.

I took the Piccadilly line in, henceforth the Stinkadilly due to the funk of BO and spices that suffused the car. Whew. Got off in Kensington, here:

I love that station. As I no doubt said before, you can just imagine Sherlock bustling in to take the tube somewhere important, the game being afoot and all that. It has

an unbelievably detailed Wikipedia page.

Strode to Dishoom. No line! Because it was a quarter to four! Delicious meal. Had the Chicken Ruby. Amazing as ever. When I was finished I had 45 minutes before the V&A closed, and I thought:

let's go get some soap.

Victory soap! I'd bought some last October and used it during the nightmare months, because it hurt my eyes and seemed appropriate for the terrible interregnum. Brisk walk in the warm afternoon sun.

The V&A is one of my favorite places:

But the new stuff should be shoveled out as soon as possible:

Says the obligatory explanatory panel:

Lovers Hold / Henry Svendsen

Lovers Hold extends Henry Svendsen's ongoing investigation into the plinth, via the spatial politics of cruising sites, reimagining sculptural supports as structure shaped by intimacy, proximity, and bodily negotiation.

Sod off with the

spatial politics of cruising sites

already.

Viscous, grotto-like forms suspended from stainless steel armatures support multiple bodies in repose, drawing on furniture designed for closeness, such as the loveseat.

Evoking the improvised nature of outdoor cruising sites

, these sculptures materialise fleeting contact as accumulated traces of desire. The work considers how bodies gather through structures not originally designed to hold them, exploring what it means to rest, lean, linger, and make contact in public space.

Incoherent nonsense dedicated to anonymous public sex. Someone sprawled on a bench after a knee-trembler, I guess. It's in the room devoted to classical statuary.

Victoria wept. Albert  frowned.

I decided to walk from the V & A to the Physical Energy statue, since a watercolor of the place is my wallpaper, seasonally altered to fit the times. It was still warm, perfect for a Kensington Park stroll, and I headed right to the statue and acted like a tourist, taking pictures.

Then it hit me: instead of walking back to Kensington and getting on the Stinkadilly line. wWas there a Lizzer near? There was. Head north and get to Paddington. On the north gate I visited the Italian gardens. Never been before. Lovely:

There's a statue of Mr. Jenner:

Wiki:

A statue of Edward Jenner, the physician, scientist and pioneer of the world's first vaccine, is located in Kensington Gardens in London. A work of the sculptor William Calder Marshall, the bronze was originally unveiled by Prince Albert in Trafalgar Square on 17 May 1858, before being moved to its present location in 1862.

He doesnât look very happy.

Many things were moved, including Queen Anne's Alcove:

That's a Chris Wren piece. More about it,

here

.

Thence to Paddington.

It does a nice enough job of incorporating the old and the new shopping areas. I had a lukewarm Americano that put me off the chain for good - three letters, canât remember, but they had power outlets, which was mostly what I was looking for. Down to the Elizabeth Line, very nice station.

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat.
items.description:
WARM BERGAMOT DAY

pt. 3.

The old church.

History:

The building originally comprised a nave and chancel, with an eighteen-bay clerestory and six-bay north and south aisles. When the prosperity of the village suffered, there were insufficient funds to maintain the church, and in the 1690s, the parish obtained permission to demolish the old church and build a much smaller one. This was funded by the sale of lead from the roofs and the bells from the tower.

I'm sure there's someone under the slab.

Brief stroll:

As I was sitting on the wall,

an old woman came over, cane in hand, not entirely steady, but not looking as though sheâd topple over. She looked at me noncommittally. I decided to sling some local lore, and just said Iâm looking for the spot where George Orwell saw the ghost. He was sitting on the wall and he saw it somewhere over there. Look, he made a map!

She looked at me, nodded, and said âIâve seen them. Iâve seen them all my life.â

It was said in a way that would be appropriate if you were remarking that you had a long lifetime acquaintance with cheddar cheese, not apparitions that proved the existence of the afterlife, or at least some persistent spiritual manifestation. I did not exactly ask her to go on, but my expression mustâve encouraged her to relate the tales, and she started with the particularly annoying spirit that lived in the house with her three children. He had a habit of opening doors, and one time her littlest somehow got out of his cradle and went across the street. This was the fault of the spirit, which may have been a gypsy, rumored to have been buried in the area. At one point, she said,  it got into bed with her, and I asked if it was just a presence or an actual manifestation or something she could see - and I was tempted to say âare you sure this just wasnât your husbandâ -  she said she could see it,  and she kicked it right out. At some point I think after it let the door open in the winter time she told her

thatâs it thatâs thatâs enough youâre out.

It left. I thought to myself well if itâs that easy, I certainly wouldâve told it straight away to be gone.

The second incident had to do with getting locked in a pub where she worked, and the owner had to come by with a key, the key didnât work in the lock. Not sure you can blame spooks for that. The ghost of the third example was in Wales, where she was living in some flats that have been knocked together, three of them, and  each had their own staircase. The third staircase on the end, the circular staircase gave her such feelings of cold, frosty dread that she could not go up it. She did eventually, and I think it turned out that a child had died in there, but there was also an old woman dressed in Victorian garb, who was sitting in a chair, quite agitated in a man with a large striped shirt and belt, came in and picked her up and took her away. The neighbors had also seen this, and were non-plus like everyone else about this. Oh, thatâs just old Jack and the lady.â There was a story about a drowned husband, a wife who refused to leave the flat, and all that.

After three stories, I was fascinated, but I also was hoping there was not a fourth since they did tend to go on. Iâll give her credit for this â years of telling  the stories over the years had taught her to boil them down to the essential details. I thanked her for her tales and moved on. Itâs possible, of course that she was a ghost herself. Townâs full of âem.

TODAY IS COOL VETIVER DAY

A walk in the woods on the penultimate day. We visited the Scottish Cows.

A mother, father, and baby. By "Baby" I mean it probably weights 700 pounds.

It's always a pleasure to head into the woods and kick the

conkers

.

I did not expect to find an old WW2 Bunker.

It was part of the

Eastern Command Line

.

One last night at the Anchor. Typical: a few people are sitting outside, and gather merry group as more people show up. I ended up talking to a guy, former ad man, who'd just sold a metric keisterload of adjustable frames to George Lucas' museum. Buoyed and chuffed by the deal. Most of the table consisted of artists from the weekend Open Studio event, and to my absolute amazement one of them said "I just bought your book." It was one of the artists - one of the brothers I mentioned yesterday. AND his wife is a big enthusiast for mid-century aspic nightmares, as well. Well that's unexpected. I said usually the guy goes to the studio and buys the artist's work, not the other way around.

A great dinner, as ever, then chatting into the evening. All done. Hard to believe it's done.

One last time before we take our leave.

items.description:
TODAY IS SPICED WOOD DAY

Itâs wood, with a spicy note.

I finished the Palin book. A nice read, as usual, a genial travelogue with some keen observations on a vast place I will never visit. I wish them all well but theyâre hard up against it. The underlying problem with Nigeria seems to be its existence, what with all the competing elements that should never have been yoked together in the first place.

In the morning I finished my column, then walked to do some drone work. Took the path across from the Tuck Shop - well, equidistant between the Tuck Shop and the Black Dog or Mucky Duck. Turn around for orientation.

Made my way past the wall of ivy buzzing with bees, turned left to skirt the field.

At one point thereâs an opening in the woods to another path that leads behind the allotments, and then to the sea. As I walked along guiding the drone, I suddenly saw -

- a woman on the screen, standing absolutely still.

I apologized and palmed the drone.

âThatâs all right,â she said. âI just wondered what that sound was.â

I said I was shooting video for a piece of music a friend had written. She nodded. Bit her apple.

âWhat kind of music?â

âPiano.â

She chewed. Paused. âJazz?â

âNo, more of a classical prelude.â

She nodded and chewed it over and apparently approved. She nodded and continued on her way.

When I got to the sea I discovered that Iâd run of storage space. When I got back I realized I hadnât removed two events.

1. The drone footage I shot the day I got the letter.

2. The shots of the house for the sales video and the Giant Swedeâs sonâs engagement party in our backyard a few days later.

I took off the new shots and wiped the card.

Went to Aldeburgh for lunch, after an interesting drive past all the construction for the new nuclear plant. They have made some nice new roundabouts. I understand this is a matter of displeasure for the locals, due to the construction and big parking lots (behind hedges, though) and even the excess of roundabouts, but if you want Net Zero and if you want to keep the lights on, well, sorry.

The lunch was in

a small cafe

in an undistinguished low building, next to a butcher and a vintage shop.

Highly recommended. Astrid had the bacon and scallops butty; I contented myself with the bacon butty.

Oh gosh. It was perfection. Iâve never had a sandwich like this. But why not? What ever kept us from just making a bacon sandwich? A little HP on the side, too.

We paid a visit to Aldeburgh proper, a handsome seaside town. Studied the Moot Court.

Wikipedia:

The building was designed in the Tudor style, built using timber frame construction techniques with wattle and daub and brick nog infilling, and was completed around 1520.

Eighty years before the first American colony.

In 1645, the building was the location for the trial, under the direction of the witchfinder general, Matthew Hopkins, of seven alleged witches who were subsequently hanged.

Witchfinder General! Thereâs a job. He was not officially entrusted as such by Parliament, though. He convicted 135 witches, a handful of which, sorry, were hanged.

Ancient proud decoration. Well, ancient by Yank standards.

Wonder what this says:

"I count only the serene or sunny hours."

Good thing to say when you're heading in for the witch trial.

A stop at the shore:

Back to the home base. Nap. Off to the Anchor for a drink before dinner -

Oh no

Sitting outside at the tables

Itâs the guy from the train

THE FOLLOWING IS AN ACCOUNT OF SMOKED OUD DAY

Iâm in a bit of a pickle here, have done absolutely nothing of interest to anyone. Weâve some jaunts planned later, I think, or maybe not. Perhaps Iâve just seen it all. That's fine. Look at that scene above. I'm happy just to be here.

Made myself a breakfast that was made all the more savory for its high ethical quotient:

I'm sure it's just a Yank perspective, but

streaky rashers

sounds so very English. Isn't that the TV show about gangsters in the 30s?

Exciting day trip: we went to Lowestoft for groceries on Wednesday. The first stop was M & S, or Marks & Spencer, or Marks & Sparks. It is not a charming locale, and the parking lot makes the average Traders Joe look like a Sam's Club expanse.

The grocery store abuts an M&S clothing store, and I picked up some nice sweaters and an eight-phial flight of menâs cologne.

The first was Smoked Oud. I had no idea what Oud was. Some kind of aromatic wood, it seems. I liked it. The clerk said that some people mix them together for their own Signature Scents, although I don't know how you'd keep track.

Me? I'm a 1 part Oud to 2 part Vetiver kind of guy

. We'll see.

The M&S branding is stark and modern, and I like it.

Yes, I always come back from trips abroad with pictures of local packaging. It's one of those delightful quirks that sets me apart! Sigh

We stopped into a local downtown shopping center, which was what youâd expect in a careworn fishing town whose piscine stocks were long ago exhausted.

It's named after

Ben

. Really. The composer was born here and died down in Aldeburgh. Walbers is equidistant between the two, so I'm sure he visited the place at some day, and might have had a pint at the Anchor.

The Centre has seen happier times.

Then to Morrisonâs, and then to Aldiâs. Dinner was a fantastic roast shoulder with okra, and we stayed up talking until late. I did not take a double sleeping-draught but nonetheless fell asleep instantly and didnât stir for eight hours. No jet lag this trip at all. It does wonders for the mood not to wake at 4:17 AM hearing pigeons hoot and coo.

TODAY IS OCEAN MUSK DAY

I have been reading Sir Michaelâs new book, â14 reasons not to go here ever no matter what others might say,â although thatâs not the official title.

He makes it sound interesting, as he has a skill for describing places with generosity and fascination, but you conclude that youâre glad he went there, not you. The book of course is personally inscribed, as are all the other Palin tomes in the Hutte bookshelf.

I should also note there is important clergy news in the Telegraph:

Chapl and Dio are the only things I could guess without googling.

This looks like the most British thing EVER.

We three went to Southwold,

where Denis got a haircut, and later we had a lunch at at the Magpies, sitting outside despite the occasional rain. If you'd like to recreate my exciting early afternoon, turn around and head up the street to Huus, and buy another Bee-themed tumbler.

By the way, if ever you're here, THIS is the place for fish and chips.

This is not in dispute.

Typical England: a reminder of something that happened three hundred years ago.

Important note from google AI: "He is distinct from William Jefferson Blythe Jr., the American biological father of former U.S. President Bill Clinton." You don't say.

"Defend They Right" is the proper order, I think. As for the reversed S? Google AI summary:

When artisans carved a metal seal matrix (stamp) in the Middle Ages, they had to engrave all letters and imagery in reverse (a mirror image) so that when it was pressed into wax, the final impression would read correctly.

The Artisan's Oversight:

Â The die-sinker accidentally carved the letter "S" facing forward on the physical stamp. Consequently, every time the seal was pressed onto an official document, it stamped out aÂ

backwards "S."

Instead of correcting the typo on a new matrix, the town kept using the seal. Over the centuries, this quirk became a beloved, permanent fixture of Southwold's civic heritage. Today, the reversed "S" is intentionally preserved and proudly displayed on theÂ

Southwold Town Hall

, the officialÂ

town signs

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Monday.
items.description:
The airport continues to lean heavily into CorpMemphisGloboHomo horrors. Nothing like committing to something thatâs both ugly and passe:

If you saw these creatures on the street you would be alarmed, and realize that a headshot would be quite difficult.

Eight PM

at the bar at the airport. The bartender has just graced me with a very heavy pour, possibly because Iâm the first person all day to sling lingo:

Double Black Jack, Neat, water back.

Usually I have a scotch on the rocks before I board if itâs an evening flight, but as you might know, the curse of metered pour means you get a washed-out drink with no character.

All signals green, so far. Birch seems to have adapted quickly to the Housesitter, because heâs not alone. Oh Iâm sure he misses me terribly! Horribly! Canât bear the pain! Or,

I like this lady. She gives me bacon. Am I alone? I am not alone. All good.

Was it here, at this very bar, that I had the bartender from Transylvania? She was fun. But I think that might have been October, and that night felt off. The whole trip felt off. Nothing felt right. I didnât need to go to England, but Iâd retired and hey letâs have fun and hop across the pond and see friends and drive around in the whole season-of-mists-and-mellow-fruitfulness thing, right? Then came The Letter.

Returning now in the damp and the chill, at least on this side, feels like returning to the scene of the crime.

Enrobed in mopery all day because I love to travel but always get verklempt the day of leaving.

Why am I doing this? Why am I leaving my life of comfortable, reassuring routine?

I cleaned the house for the sitter, took Birch out when the rain paused. It was odd how swiftly the world turned chilly and wet, and while I know there will be warmth and sun again before winter moves in, the break is a necessary slap to dispel all the dreams and fancies. Stand up and pay attention.

What I want the most, of course, is slumber. I want to get on that plane and ride up into the heavens, put on my earphones and get as much as sleep as I can. Tomorrow is a trial. Three hours after touchdown to get through customs, collect bags, get on the Elizabeth Line and rattle off to Liverpool Street Station. Should be plenty of time. Then the train to Ipswich, where we do . . .

Do you know by now?

Thatâs the tick-tight timing problem right there, but once I get that sorted itâs just a matter of keeping awake until Darsham.

Google Street View of the lovely environs of Darsham:

This isnât one of those get-me-to-the-Anchor missions. After Natalie left for Brazil, yes. Last Christmas, yes. And I just remembered: last Christmas I was still engaged in the faux-marriage thing where we texted  back and forth, because I still didnât really believe this was all going to happen.

And now she doesnât exist.

So thatâs my mood on the start of this trip. Backward looking and I donât like that at all.

11:35

Off and away.

4:31 AM

I slept a solid three and a half hours, which is pretty good for this flight. Wasnât the most solid, restful sleep, given the postures one assumes to sleep in a chair crammed against the wall,  but itâll do. Now awaiting the breakfast cart, which I trust is nigh. I should set my clocks ahead. Align myself to GMT. Knowing it's actually 4:32 is not a good thing.

Let's open the shade and look outside . . . . AAAAIEEEEE

HOW CAN THIS BE? IT'S FOUR THIRTY IN THE MORNING AND DARK IN THIS CLOSE LONG TUBE

5:36, aka 11:37:

Oh my stars and bars

I WENT BACK TO SLEEP

I guess packing one of Birch's phenobarbital pills was the right decision! Total game-changer! Kidding. I had planned the whole day this way, waking early, no nap, generous whiskey = snoozin by midnight. If it works, good. If not, thou art well and truly hosed.

To the surprise of no one who has ever taken this flight before, breakfast was a chewy egg-and-cheese âcalzone,â with a cup of yogurt. It was fine, because I brought a packet of Cholula in anticipation of this exact moment, and was able to add flavor and heat to the sodden carb log.

The plates have been cleared and we are now heading fast towards Heathrow. We will arrive new to a day that's already half gone.

Looking forwards first to that nice little cigar moment prior to the Lizzie Whizzer, then the coffee at the station. Costa? If Iâm pressed. Not the best but not everyone can be Nero. As Nero himself no doubt reminded people.

LATER: And so, as it was prophesized, it came to pass! In other words, they said we would land, and we did.

2:12 PM

Liverpool Street Station, NERO Coffee Shop.

As we waited to deplane I talked with my seat mate, a statuesque young woman whoâd been to Minnesota to see her grandparents. (Who are probably my age.) Theyâd gone to a Vikings game at the stadium, and she was still in awe of the show and spectacle and wondrous noise. Once off I power walked past half the plane to passport control. The line consisted of three people. Bag was out in ten minutes. Out, around the corner, over to the Sinnerâs Area, enjoy the little cigar, then back down into the depths - down the corridor, turn left, beep the phone, into the lift, down, out, left to the platform. The Elizabeth Line or Lizzie Whizzer was along in five minutes, and the trip into town seemed half the 50 minutes it actually took.

Went outside to finish the post-journey cigar. Fell into talking with a gentleman who was standing outside having a cup of coffee; he heard my accent, asked if I was from America, and said he loved America.

We all do,

he said.

Welcome to Gary, Indiana.

It may seem masochistic of me, but I think it's important. Google Street view has done more to document urban devolvement than anything else. In the 60s the government sent a guy around with a camera. Now we have everything.

And all of this is voluntary. Bad decisions by government, abandonment by owners due to financial problems or the inability to make a living in the neighborhood, and of course the work of strippers and  vandals, and the people in the neighborhood who prey on others and make the area economically unviable.

The empire

packed up and left long ago:

A few elements of elegance remain, probably because terra-cotta has no resale value and no one wants one of these decorations in their living room.

A 20s commercial structure with a post-war renovation.

Four storefronts for sale!

Oh well

Yes, it's the same building. For some reason the owner reconfigured the front.

Reviews of the Budget Motel

are not enthusiastic.

Oh my God

There are plans underway to renovate it, supposedly. Housing, I think.

Needs a good scrubbing.

That's nice but it doesn't pay the taxes.

The bland blank wall lends itself well to absolute dystopian decay:

Wigs, once. Wigs, no more.

The art of the building, the language, the history, appers lost on some people.

Ah - an old remnant piece of signage.

Oh well

At least it's still -

Oh well

An old sign, revealed:

Signs of a renovation. Literally, I guess. Eventually the glue failed.

Not its finest era, perhaps:

Well, that's solved

Even the old solid government buildings are empty and sullied:

In a similar theme of old authorites fleeing and leaving their offices to the mercies of time and vandals:

Wikipedia:

"The City Methodist Church, latterly known as City United Methodist Church is a disused church in Gary, Indiana, United States. Once the largest Methodist church in the Midwest, it ceased as a place of worship in 1975, after just over 50 years of use."

In England, something like this would be 500 years old, not 50s, and it would've been knocked down by order of a king.

You wonder if it will all just fall apart and that will be that.

Googling around for the general concept of 1920s Detroit apartment buildings, I got a hit:

That helped. Itâs still around, and itâs a class joint, as they say. Thatâs great!

I started poking around the neighborhood to see what itâs like, and - as always - found one of those jaw-dropping sets of ruined areas, with dessicated, stripped hulks next to works of transcendent magnificence.

Detroit just makes me mad.

The hotel:

according to this history

Annnnd I'm off for a while. You know I need this. I have been going pell-mell for the entire summer.

Well, not pell-mell by some peopleâs standards, because Iâve taken naps, and looked at Twitter, but mentally pell-mell. As I mentioned before, everything has been forward-organized, forward-centered. I take Birch out for the morning pee and Iâm thinking about the 11 AM deadline, but before that, the 9-10 AM website work. On Sunday I was at the Giant Swedeâs for football, and mentioned that I had two deadlines that night, and he noted, spreading his arms to encompass all present (which included Sam, another Valli Denizen of the old days), noting that we were all retired but I was the only one still working. It was a compliment. Now, the Giant Swede worked in the same sense as the Ex worked, which is to say, hard, laboring over company politics and policies. I have never worked like that. My work is âcoming up with stuff, often.â Itâs not the same. But without the work and the forward organizing, I donât know what I would do.

Well! Iâm about to find out.

I should note that the game was, in the end, a great joy - an experience born in the cauldron of despair, but lifted to great heights on the gusts of grit, determination, and fortuitous referee calls. The moment when victory seems possible, the moment when a score is made that might turn the tide, and the Crazy Uke bursts out with the ON THE ROAD TO VICTORY song and we clink glasses - ah. Fall is here and Sundays have new weight and purpose. And Iâm pretty sure it will be a disappointing season, but we endure the troughs to earn the crisp air of Valhalla, right?  If not, thereâs pizza and aquavit.

It was a good weekend, all told. The annual Dog Festival was Saturday, over at the Finch, and Birch - not in costume, hence ineligible - made a pest of himself once he realized there were treats unstinting, so we left after a while, not running into The Attractive Divorcee. (Thereâs always the possibility of running into her tomorrow morn in the elevator like last Monday, not that Iâm setting my watch.) She just got the most remarkable opportunity. I mean . . . my gosh. Iâm watching her soar on every front.

On Saturday Birch and I took walks to Centennial Lakes, which was hosting a crafts and arts festival - BAD IDEA WITH DOG - and we did the circuit at sunset. The temps had dropped in a way that says âokay, that week of 80s, that was the result of a bureaucratic oversight. Now weâre serious about fall.â The chill sets in at night and the chill now greets you in the morn.

But the worldâs still green. Forward.

HIATALLY COMMENCING NOW.

Promise!

everyoneâs

just fascinated by Jack Paar

He was so open and vulnerable! âUnpredictable, emotional and principled,â as   his Wiki bio says.

are

they saying?

As Goodman's fame grew, she became difficult to handle on the show, and Paar was not happy with her upstaging habits. She would 'top' his jokes. Commenting on another guest one evening, Paar quipped "Give them enough rope," "And they'll skip," ad-libbed Goodman, brightly. isnât what you might think.

Six months ago, this pretty young lady, who is still a student of foreign languages with a year to go for graduation, won a job working evenings as an announcer at a local TV station.

The contest was announced in a newspaper. Those wishing to compete were to write a letter to the station, state their qualifications and enclose a picture. Of more than a hundred applicants, this girl was one of the few called in for personal interviews by the television-station executives.

Dum-dum DUMMMMMMM

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Wednesday.
items.description:
And now the crushing return

to brooding dissatisfaction after the sugar-high exultation of success! No, not really. Not at all. I should be more even tempereed. The good news is that the baseline is, more or less, mute numb acceptance.

Daughter is in Portugal, and not exactly doing a bang-up job of sending pictures, so Iâm using the Find My Friends feature and Google street view to see where she is. This is the modern world: you can wait for the location on the other side of the world to refresh, then move down the same street on your computer screen. This is quite different from my early days, when you simply vanished, and returned at some point, and then six days later, had 36 pictures to share.

In other news: the freezer door was slightly ajar again today, ruining the frozen yogurt and the French fries. Everything else was still solid. I tire of this. I especially tire of it when itâs a Designated Ice Cream night. I was loath to go to the store because I had a good parking spot in the garage, but Iâm not going to be without that delicious sea-salt and caramel truffle ice cream. Has to be sea-salt! Canât be any other kind of sodium chloride. I want to taste the brine and the whale pee.

Yes, I know, thereâs a difference. I was looking at some Williams-Sonoma sea salt, and itâs $30. Why? Because it has a Williams-Sonoma label on it. When you open your cupboard and everything has a consistent label you are reminded and reassured of your class status.

Anyway.  I checked all the apps to see A) if the product existed, and B) who had it. Lundsnbyerlys FTW as we used to say, ironically of course. It was 6.49. I get to the store, find it. Itâs $7.39. Hmm. I call up the app: it says $6.49. Thus armored, I go to self-checkout, ready to provide full documentation if it rings up wrong. It did not ring up wrong.

WAIT HOLD ON, you say. What about the half-price carts?

Surprisingly little. And strange choices. Did Bean Season just end?

Anyway, that was that. Drove home to a gaseous track from the last mostly-meh album by Kinobe. Now sitting outside on the balcony because itâs still warm, and it wonât be warm forever.

Today in AI Restoration:

I dialed down the color a bit. The original result was much brighter. (

Here it is, embiggened

, if you like.) The site today:

It's Block E, site of a massive failed development. Another angle of the site a few years later, also colorized:

Larger version,

here

. If it looks familiar, it's because we saw an animated version last June. Everything the AI

invents

is wrong.

The hallucinations are vexatious. I can't blame it for the one above, since I gave it nothing to go on, and didn't tell it about the Bridgeman's restaurant and the Gopher theater. If the picture is blurry, the AI will invent things like rugs or tiles.

Which do you prefer?

The first one is the accurate image. It maintains the gauzy evocative romantic tone of the original. The second one, made in Nano B, couldn't resist improving as much as possible.

It was the Crane plumbing showroom on the Boardwalk on Atlantic City, back in the day when companies built things like these for the public's fleeting delight. You entered the showroom through a large pipe.

As long as we're on the subject of technology and things in need of proper pipes for flushing . . .

I'd say 98% of the population doesn't use AI, except to read Google answers to queries, or chatting with a bot in automated help chat boxes. Most people are not setting up agents or having Claude book airplaines. But they do see AI generated images - cartoons, signs, ads - and for the most part, they're tired of it. I use it for fun, but we all know it's a jape. I stick my buffed-up AI version in the scenarios to illustrate the column, because otherwise there's no art at all, or, I'd be using AI illustrations without demonstrating any self-awareness of the ridiculousness of it all.

That said: Thereâs a lot here.

First of all, the cartoonist is a terribly unfunny woman who posts straw man comics to demonstrate her own moral superiority. âPizzacake.â Thatâs about as tumblry a name as it got back in 2011. Second, I agree with the basic idea: AI menu art can be absolutely ghastly. I wrote about this on the Substack a few times.  The debate sometimes veers into the sameness of AI generated menu design, but itâs mostly about the food. By which I mean the âfood.â

The cartoon appeared in a subreddit devoted to âdefending AI,â and itâs populated by the absolute summation of the Redditor Archetype: self-regarding midwit fedora-tippers who spend their time generating

amile shite-pix of buxom catgirls

, and are absolutely completely and utterly convinced that they are creatives. The prompt is an act of creativity equal to wielding a brush or a pen on a tablet. Anyone who says otherwise is an envious gatekeeper - and theyâre willfully lying about how good it is!

(Note: I hate the style no matter who or what produces it. The ridiculous big glossy eyes, the tiny features, the ever-pointed chin. It's all so tiresome.)

They are keen on branding the critics of their catgirls as ANTIs, guilty of Luddite Logic. The opponents are always mad and shouting, and the AI Kids are always cool and composed.

Itâs not that people hate THE ENTIRE CONCEPT of AI Art. No cares theyâre making their anime cliches so they can pose them as they wish.

Everyone else is rolling their eyes at actual adults who do this stuff. We're laughing at the guys who don't get the references:

The main annoyance: their insistence on being equivalent to people with talent who have taken the time to master a craft.

As Iâve probably said before elsewhere, or maybe not, who knows or cares, the only AI art that will rise to the level of Actual Art will be movies, because rhat will require a certain set of artistic skills. Composition, writing, lighting, pacing, editing. If you leave all that to AI itâll be off, and weâll know itâs off. Someone will might an AI movie starring Humphrey Bogart, but theyâll have to understand things the AI never will. The way rue inhabits a manâs face while it remains utterly blank. The way loss is expressed at the back of the eyes.

It'll get there. But you suspect it will be drowned out by the onslaught of shiny falsehoods that characterize the look of the culture now. I hate it.

This world is fake, and everyone knows it, and it's making the culture hollow, alienating, and just damned

wrong.

Fargin' Temu Matrix.

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Tuesday.
items.description:
The Slough of Despond

is looking rather . . . verdant, but I expect the final iteration of Sunderwood Park will feature clear pristine ponds. Birch and I took an early walk today, since the day was rearranged by a Labor Day party at the Crazy Uke's. Great time. An absolute tonic. I drove back having a rare Car Cigar, listening to

good driving music

(wind it up in fourth gear, drop it into fifth at :52), mien set in a stoic mask I learned from Sonny Crockett. Drove fast and took the turns so I felt some G-force.

Since I'd had a big late lunch - a polish and a hot dog expertly charred by the Crazy Uke's grillmaster son - we walked before supper, and had our goodbye to summer. Rambled through the scrubs and brambles, scampered to the highest point - admittedly not much, but I felt like doing a Rocky bounce at the top: we'd made it through the summer, we survived, we were

here

, and here was good. Not just

okay

. It's

good

. Elevator chat this morning with The Attractive Divorcee, field chats with other dog owners who both said "Hello Birch!" and a hallway colloquy with Jerome from NYC and the Fun Couple down the hall. I say it and people laugh but I'm serious.

The Fred saved my life.

The Answer

to yesterday's riddle, of course, was Cliff Arquette. I heard his name at the end of the credits and was surprised to learn he'd done an old radio Dragnet. The tic-tac-toe grid showed his position in the Hollywood Squares as Charley Weaver; the Toto album had a song supposedly named after his granddaughter Rosanne, although that's in dispute.

Had a nice visit

from a friend (and Bleatnik) who stopped by Saturday with many, many tomatoes. Look at this perfection:

There were other varities, including the San Marzano. Now I have to make sauce, lots of it, and freeze it. No, that's not right. Now I am lucky enough to make sauce. It's not that much work. You chop them up and add a jar of Prego, and you're good.

(let us wait for the screaming to subside)

Of course I would not do that. I'm not even using jarlic.

I would like one of these.

But why? Theyâre small.

Maybe thatâs it. Something compact, easy to keep orderly. Iâm not crazy about the small windows in the bedrooms, but the big windows are nice . . . except youâd have to keep the drapes shut all the time, right? We had big picture windows in the front room, and they were never undraped, because that was being on display, as I was reminded. We had sheer drapes that let you see the world beyond through a gauzy scrim, and the cat was always going to town with his claws on the drapes, so my Mother had to fix them with a needle and thread. I remember the drapes closed most of the time, especially in the evening . . . which was odd, because no one was ever in the living room in the evening. Everyone was in the basement, the knotty-pine basement, watching the Quasar from reclining chairs.

In short thereâs almost nothing about that I want today. But I did love the kitchen, with its push-button GE electric stove and range built into the wall, the boomerang-patterned Formica counter, the blonde-wood cabinets with the slender brass handles. It was refreshed in the 80s, and it wasnât done very well. The old bad wallpaper was replaced with new bad wallpaper. Is it fair to say one's dear forebearers had questionable taste? After all, who am I to say? I wasn't there in 1962 when people were convinced that Pennsylvania Dutch wallpaper patterns went with copper appliances and turquoise Formica. (As we will see below the fold, as it turns out. I didn't plan that!)

But. If I found something like this . . .

Too bad they don't exist any -

Iâd be tempted. Itâs returning to the original home. Back to the cradle. And thatâs just pathetic, in a way. Itâs a retreat. An admission that n to only can you go home again, you have to: I had run as far as I could but there was always an invisible elastic band that would snap me back at some point.

More than that, though, thereâs what this all represented, once. Something new and modern. Something apart,  but aligned with others of similar intentions. All of the assumptions that these houses contain are the assumptions with which I grew up. OH YOU MEAN WHITE FLIGHT AND SUBURBAN ALIENATION

<perry_stare.jpg>

Yeah right thatâs exactly it

Itâs all very amusing considering that I am in the ultra-modern monochrome FRED BASE ONE (monochrome with splashes of color, though, remember that) and I love it. This is the opposite of the Arts & Crafts Jasperwood, which was heaven. This is not a decompression tank; this is total Etch-a-Sketch shake. I can chose any paradigm going forward, any stage set I wish to dress. If I had complete and total druthers, delivered by Druthers-4-U, it would be a stark and refined 1930s house I would outfit like a new London club for men that opened in 1937. Big round chairs, elegant zinc floor ashtrays, travel posters that nodded towards the abstract but were still representational, a silver statuette of a gazelle, that sort of thing. Who knows. Weâll see. There arenât any 30s houses in the burbs. There arenât many in Minneapolis. All the new construction I see consists of garage-forward dullards in treeless developments.

Something else Iâve noticed. It haunts me. It suggests that these houses have been bought by some massive secret Blackstone project that has a template for updating.

Itâs this thing. I have this now, in the Fred. It's everywhere.

To my surprise I saw it at some in-laws back in November.

I will not live with this thing.

Itâs not that it doesnât do the job - but that dead head with its small control panel, the cheap membrane entry-pad, the LED lights from the clock radio you had in 1981 - No.

I am watching the 3d season of

Silo

out of grim duty. It's ugly and everyone in the show is beaten and grimy and unattractive. The show worked for two seasons because it was headed somewhere and delivered good cliffhangers that moved it along with confidence. Since the show is based on books, there's an END coming, and we are guarateed of a conclusion. Great! But this season is tiresome water-treading. The main star, who has refined her entier performance down to "irritated confusion," has amnesia, the hoariest trope in the book. At least we go back to the past before Solo Times, and meet a pilot who went on a secret mission against Iran, survived, and has . . . AMNESIA!

I should note the other irritating thing: the pilot of the fighter jet is of course a young beautiful female who's AWESOME and we know that because she is an unfriendly, abrasive bitch. Her brother, a congressman, is helping a reporter Learn the Truth, and the reporter is awesome and dedicated and fierce necause she too is an unfriendly, abrasive bitch. No, I'm not saying female characters have to be likeable and pliable. I'm saying they should be written by people who know how to communicate strength and intelligence with interesting charactereistics. Oh she snaps at everyone because no one understands her tremendous burdens. No, she's just an unpleasent person.

items.title: LILEKS (James) :: The Bleat for Friday.
items.description:
I was looking up

more things in Fargo, and thought Iâd use Google street view to see the house where I grew up.

Itâs blurred. An interdimentional rift has settled over the place, and the strange and incomprehensible shapes on the other side shimmer and glow. Or, something was on the camera lens.

Hey, wait a minute

I used to look at my house on Street View and see the whole thing. Turns out that this is a feature Google provides: you can request your domicile be blocked for all time, and the block extends backwards in time as well. The neighbors to the north must have done it. I can think of no better way to make people wonder what youâre up to.

But thatâs not fair. Itâs natural to think that, and also what the Redditors would say is a sign of

copbrain

- they love the -brain suffix - but thereâs no reason you have to submit to the indifferent eye of the Google Cars.

That banner above couldâve been me in 1967 or so. Thereâs something bittersweet about being caught like that in an unguarded moment of sudden wonder, looking at the car:

what is that thing? Is it from the future? Jeepers, itâs cool

Of course no kid says jeepers anymore.

Ordinary day.

No seizures. Woke, ate my usual omelette with relish, but not in the hotdog sense,   then emembered that the water was going to be shut off today for five hours. I filled the water bowl and coffee maker and then discovered . . . well, sorry no, I need that for the Friday column. Did the Gallery of Regrettable Food Substack,  had a boring lunch, filed the weekend NRO column with a note to the editor that it was dark and bitter enough to be passed off as boiled-down Turkish coffee.

By the way, a kind letter-writer this week said he hoped NR was paying me well. Hah! Youâd be surprised how little they pay. But itâs something, and everything helps.

HOT. Birch did not want to take a walk to Centennial Lakes today. We got a ways into the park, and he stopped: nope. Might have been the storm clouds. He wanted to go back into the cool car, so we did. Some grocery shopping, home, nap, steak, radio show, walk. You can see the strange structures going up in Sunderwood Park:

I would also like to note that he has made an appropriate protest to the sticks that make up the new fence. TROPHY STRUT!

Ordinary in every way, except for a curious lack of mental fugue recitations of grievances and slights and hurts and such. I still feel like Iâm the bad guy for not working on a future relationship, for not being concerned about how sheâs doing,  but I have to remember she was the one who sang

Heave ho, Heave Ho, itâs Off to Fred You Go.

Divorced people who got the big nix know you exist in a state of tremulous connection for a long time. The

fact

of being over is not enough. Itâs not over until many things click into place and other things settle like sediment. There was one other time in my life I knew something was over, but it happened in advance.

Saturday night I tried to find the tune I heard when I realized that the most important part of my life was done. Itâs one of those moments that hits you with such clarity, with such unexpected force, that you know itâs absolutely true, and youâd best open up and let it in. I remembered it last Saturday night because I was up, and got myself a Grantâs.

Back up: Mad magazine used to do ad parodies, and when I was a kid reading Mad I didnât necessarily know the original reference. But I remember they did a parody of a Grantâs whiskey ad, the tagline of which was âAs long as youâre up, get a me a Grantâs.â Great Don-Draper era stuff. I know I've mentioned this before, because when I searched for ads a 2019 Bleat came up. Now I've given it hues:

I have been a Grantâs fan since 2016, when I sat down at the bar at Washington National Airport and looked at the whiskey list and settled on the Grantâs, simply because I was remembering a parody of an ad Iâd never seen. When I sipped the drink it struck me as uniquely delicious. I was tired and we still had the flight home to come, and it had

been a day

. This reward . . . it was marvelous. At the time. Itâs reasonably good blended Scotch. Iâve had a bottle in the cupboard ever since.

I can see the terminal now - a futuristic circular space I visited when I lived in DC, because this was where the flights back to MSP originated. You had to go down a tunnel to get to it. The walls sloped to meet the floor.

(Video framegrab from 1992)

Now I was back, two decades later, accompanied by Daughter and Emma, the French Foreign Exchange student. Weâd taken her to DC, and then-Wife had gone back to Minneapolis, after which I took the girls to New York. Weâd stayed in the Roger Smith, my old home, and had a suite on the top floor with a dining room and a living room, upgraded perhaps because they looked at my history and saw Iâd been staying there since the Stone Age. I had to tell the girls that this was not the standard New York hotel experience. Youâre getting something special. We wandered around the bright blaring lights of Times Square on warm night, Rockefeller Center, all the Gotham glories. The day we left began in the sweltering and odiferous hell of Penn Station, where we took the fast train down to DC to head back home.

Iâd taken that train many times. I hadnât lived in DC for years but it still had its pull. I was sitting a row back from the girls, and listening to a Pat Metheny playlist, and a composition came up - it struck, deep, as some of his work does, and I remember looking at the world flashing past outside the window, and Natalie and Emma talking and laughing, and I knew that even though her graduation was two years away, the character of Fatherhood as Iâd known it was already done and dusted. It was just playing out the coda now.

Of course, thereâd be so much more. The hell-summer of 2017 with the search for Ghost Scout. The rituals of the senior year. The meetings for the Rotary trip that would beam her out of my life entirely. The addition of Birch. But that was clean-up. On that train,  with that composition playing, the sight of her confident and laughing and happy  - I knew my job was done.

Of course, itâs never done.

But you know what I mean. Itâs all details and repetition and reinforcement from now on. The realization that this phase was done felt final and inarguable, and it was right there that I knew the autumn of my life had begun.

Sitting on the balcony looking west on a summer Saturday night, sipping a Grantâs, listening to Metheny, I thought: I was absolutely right.

Let's lighten the mood with some Amazon Krep! I was looking at toasters for The Last House, since the Bella is so light you sneeze and knock it over, and I want something substantial and dependable. I'd considered a Cuisinart, but the reviews make me wary. I think it's best to avoid their electronics.

Amazon suggested somthing that looked nifty! And look what you get!
